course.title: Modern HTML & CSS
course.shortDescription: Build real web pages from scratch — semantic HTML, the CSS box model, layout, responsive design, and animation, with live in-browser coding labs.
course.longDescription:
This showcase course walks you through the complete freeCodeCamp Learn HTML5 and CSS3 From Scratch curriculum, split into focused video segments with readings, quizzes, and live Web labs in between. You will write markup and styles directly in the Mentrily web editor and see your pages render instantly.

By the end you will be able to structure a page with semantic HTML, style it with modern CSS (colors, units, typography, the box model), lay it out with display modes, positioning and media queries, and polish it with transitions, animations, and CSS variables.
course.courseSummary: Semantic HTML, forms, CSS selectors and specificity, colors and units, typography, the box model, display and positioning, backgrounds, media queries, transitions and animations, CSS variables.

content.description: Set up your tools and write your very first HTML document.
content.problemStatement: Set up your tools and write your very first HTML document.

contentBlocks.content:
What HTML actually is

HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is not a programming language — it is a markup language that describes the structure and meaning of content. Every page you have ever visited is, underneath, an HTML document that the browser parses into a tree of elements (the DOM) and then renders.

In this first segment you will install the tools professionals use every day — Google Chrome and Visual Studio Code — create a project folder, and write a complete HTML document with the standard skeleton: <!DOCTYPE html>, <html>, <head>, and <body>.

  • Watch for: why the <head> holds metadata the user never sees
  • Watch for: how Live Server refreshes your page automatically
  • Watch for: heading levels h1–h6 and why a page should have exactly one h1

Key takeaways

Every HTML document starts with a doctype, wraps everything in <html>, keeps metadata in <head>, and puts visible content in <body>. Emmet abbreviations (like typing ! then Tab) generate this skeleton instantly. Keep this structure in your head — the quiz after the next segment will test it.

content.description: The core content elements: headings, paragraphs, images, links, lists, and tables.
content.problemStatement: The core content elements: headings, paragraphs, images, links, lists, and tables.

contentBlocks.content:
Content elements — the 90% you use daily

Most real-world markup is a small vocabulary used well: headings, paragraphs, images, and anchors. This segment covers all of them, plus the details that separate beginners from professionals: relative vs. absolute paths for images, the alt attribute, target="_blank" for external links, and in-page anchor links with #id.

  • Watch for: why white space collapses in HTML
  • Watch for: the difference between <strong>/<em> (semantic) and bold/italic (visual)
  • Watch for: ordered vs. unordered vs. nested lists, and basic <table> structure

Professional habit

Always write meaningful alt text for images. Screen readers speak it aloud, search engines index it, and it renders when the image fails to load. An image that is purely decorative gets an empty alt="" — never omit the attribute entirely.

content.problemStatement: Collect user input with forms, then speed up your editing with Prettier, shortcuts, and Emmet.

contentBlocks.content:
Forms: where HTML meets your users

Forms are how the web collects data — logins, checkouts, sign-ups. The essentials: a <form> wrapper, <input> elements with the right type (text, email, password, radio, checkbox), <textarea> for long text, and a submit control. Two attributes make or break a form: name (the key the server receives) and the <label>'s for attribute (accessibility and bigger click targets).

  • Watch for: why radio buttons only group when they share the same name
  • Watch for: Prettier auto-formatting on save and the productivity shortcuts segment

From elements to a real site

Knowing elements is one thing — combining them into a coherent multi-page site is where it clicks. This project builds a small site with a logo, navigation, home, about, numbers, and contact pages, all linked together with relative paths.

content.description: How CSS attaches to HTML: inline, internal, and external styles; selectors; inheritance; and specificity.
content.problemStatement: How CSS attaches to HTML: inline, internal, and external styles; selectors; inheritance; and specificity.

contentBlocks.content:
The Cascade is the whole game

CSS stands for Cascading Style Sheets, and the cascade — which rule wins when several apply — is the single most important mental model in CSS. This segment covers the three ways to attach styles (inline, internal <style>, external .css file), element/class/id selectors, grouping, inheritance, and the specificity hierarchy.

  • Watch for: why external stylesheets are the professional default
  • Watch for: the "power struggle" — inline beats id, id beats class, class beats element
  • Watch for: which properties inherit (text-related) and which do not (box-related)

Specificity cheat-sheet

From weakest to strongest: universal selector * → element (p) → class (.card) → id (#hero) → inline style="". When specificity ties, the last rule declared wins. Reach for classes by default; ids and inline styles make overrides painful.

content.description: Color names, RGB, RGBA, and hex; then px, %, em, rem, vh and vw — and when to use each.
content.problemStatement: Color names, RGB, RGBA, and hex; then px, %, em, rem, vh and vw — and when to use each.

contentBlocks.content:
Colors and units — the vocabulary of visual CSS

Two systems you will use constantly: color notations (named colors, rgb(), rgba() with alpha transparency, and 6-digit hex like #008d98) and measurement units. The unit rules that matter in practice:

  • px — fixed size, ignores user font preferences
  • em — relative to the parent's font size (compounds when nested!)
  • rem — relative to the root font size (predictable — the modern default)
  • vh/vw — percentages of the viewport, perfect for full-screen heroes

content.description: Font stacks, Google Fonts, and text properties — then padding, margin, and border: the box model.
content.problemStatement: Font stacks, Google Fonts, and text properties — then padding, margin, and border: the box model.

contentBlocks.content:
Every element is a box

The box model is the foundation of all CSS layout: content, wrapped in padding (space inside the border), then border, then margin (space outside). This segment also covers professional typography: font-family stacks with generic fallbacks, loading Google Fonts, font-weight and font-style, and text alignment properties.

  • Watch for: shorthand order — padding: top right bottom left (clockwise)
  • Watch for: margin collapsing between vertical neighbors
  • Watch for: border-radius and how 50% makes a circle

content.description: Block vs inline vs inline-block, centering, box-sizing, and the full background-image toolkit including gradients.
content.problemStatement: Block vs inline vs inline-block, centering, box-sizing, and the full background-image toolkit including gradients.

contentBlocks.content:
Display: how boxes flow

display decides whether an element stacks (block), flows within text (inline), or does both (inline-block). Combined with box-sizing: border-box — which makes width include padding and border — these are the properties that make layouts predictable. The second half of this segment covers background images: background-size: cover, positioning, fixed attachment for parallax feels, and linear-gradient overlays for readable hero text.

  • Watch for: the classic mobile navbar example
  • Watch for: layering a gradient over an image in one background declaration

content.description: Float, the four position values, media queries for responsive layouts, and stacking with z-index.
content.problemStatement: Float, the four position values, media queries for responsive layouts, and stacking with z-index.

contentBlocks.content:
Taking elements out of the flow

position: relative nudges an element while keeping its space; absolute removes it from the flow and anchors it to the nearest positioned ancestor; fixed pins it to the viewport (sticky navbars). Then the big one: media queries — @media (min-width: 768px) { ... } — the mechanism behind every responsive site. Finally, z-index controls stacking, and ::before/::after pseudo-elements inject decorative content without extra markup.

  • Watch for: why absolute children need a relative parent
  • Watch for: mobile-first vs desktop-first query strategies

content.description: Advanced selectors and pseudo-classes, then motion: transform, transition, and keyframe animations.
content.problemStatement: Advanced selectors and pseudo-classes, then motion: transform, transition, and keyframe animations.

contentBlocks.content:
Motion with intent

Modern interfaces feel alive because of three tools: transform (translate, scale, rotate, skew — GPU-accelerated, layout-safe), transition (smooth interpolation between states, usually on :hover), and @keyframes animations for anything looping or multi-step. Before the motion section, this segment tightens your selector game: descendant vs child combinators, :hover, link states, and :root.

  • Watch for: why animating transform outperforms animating top/left
  • Watch for: animation-fill-mode keeping the final keyframe state

content.description: CSS variables, icon fonts, shadows, browser prefixes, semantic tags, and the Emmet workflow — the professional finishing kit.
content.problemStatement: CSS variables, icon fonts, shadows, browser prefixes, semantic tags, and the Emmet workflow — the professional finishing kit.

contentBlocks.content:
The professional finishing kit

The final segment introduces CSS custom properties (variables) — define --brand: #008d98 once on :root and reuse it everywhere with var(--brand) — the technique every design system, including the one rendering this page, is built on. Plus Font Awesome icons, text-shadow/box-shadow for depth, and semantic tags (header, main, section, footer) for accessible structure.

You made it

You have now covered the entire 11.5-hour curriculum. The final exam ahead has 10 concept questions and one hands-on build challenge. You need 75% to pass, and you have 2 attempts — review the specificity, box-model, and units quizzes before you start.
